terms.means: Cut into small cubes about the size of a pea. Try to make them all close to the same size so they cook evenly.
Chop into tiny bits, smaller than a grain of rice. Keep rocking the knife back and forth over the pile until nothing big is left.
Cut into rough, bite-size pieces. They don't have to match.
Cut into flat pieces, like slices of bread.
Cut into thin sticks, about the size of a matchstick.
How chefs hold a knife: thumb and bent pointer finger pinch the blade just in front of the handle, and the other fingers wrap the handle. It steers the tip exactly where you aim.
How your other hand holds food for cutting: fingertips curled under, knuckles forward, and the flat of the blade resting against your knuckles. The knife can't reach your fingertips.
Run a knife's edge along a honing steel to push it back into line. It keeps a knife sharp between sharpenings, and you can do it every time you cook.
A flat slice cut the long way, the first step of a dice or julienne. Even planks make even sticks and cubes.
The finest dice: cubes about ⅛ inch on every side, cut from a julienne.
Sticks about ¼ inch thick and 2 to 3 inches long. Cut across, they make a small dice.
Leaves stacked, rolled up tight, and sliced across into thin ribbons. Used for basil, mint, and greens.
Rub food down a grater so it falls off in shreds. The big holes make shreds. The small holes make a paste.
Grate just the colored outside of a lemon or orange peel. Stop when you see white; the white part tastes bitter.
Cook a liquid with small, lazy bubbles that pop now and then. If big bubbles roll all over, turn the heat down.
Big bubbles rolling all over the pot, even while you stir.
Cook gently in liquid that's barely bubbling.
Cook in a little hot oil or butter, stirring often.
Cook in a very hot pan without moving the food, so the outside turns deep brown.
Brown the food first, then cook it slowly with a little liquid and the lid on until it's very tender.
Soak food in a flavorful liquid, called a marinade, before you cook it.
Stir fast in little circles with a whisk or a fork, to mix things together and add air.
Beat soft butter and sugar together hard until the mixture is fluffy and a little paler.
Lay the dough over itself in layers, like folding a letter to fit in an envelope.
Push the dough away with the heel of your hand, fold it back, turn it, and repeat until it's smooth and stretchy.
Let shaped dough rise a second time before it bakes, until it's puffy and a gentle poke springs back slowly.
Wake an ingredient up before it goes in. Yeast blooms in warm water until it foams, which shows it's alive. Spices bloom in hot oil until they smell strong.
Dough that has just come together: rough, lumpy, and sticky, with dry bits still showing. Kneading turns it smooth.
Slightly sticky. A tacky dough grabs your finger for a moment, then lets go clean, without leaving dough behind.
Stretch a small piece of dough slowly between your fingers. If it goes thin enough to see light through without tearing, it's kneaded enough.
A beaten egg, often with a spoonful of water, brushed on dough before baking so the crust turns shiny and golden.
Press a floured fingertip into rising dough. If the dent springs back slowly and leaves a small mark, it's ready to bake. Springs back fast: wait longer. Doesn't spring back: it's gone too far.
The soft inside of a bread or cake, and the pattern of holes you see when you slice it.
A yeast dough made richer with fat, eggs, sugar, or milk, like challah or dinner rolls. It bakes softer and browns faster than a lean dough of flour, water, yeast, and salt.
Sprinkle a thin, light layer, like flour on the counter so dough doesn't stick.
Gently lift and turn the food so every piece gets coated, like tossing a salad.
Hot oil looks wavy and rippled on top. That means it's hot enough for the food.
Meat has thin lines running through it, like the lines in wood. Cut across those lines, not along them, so each bite is tender.
Butter and flour cooked together, stirring, for a few minutes. It thickens milk or broth into a smooth sauce. Say it "roo."
Cook something for just a minute or two in boiling water, then scoop it straight into a bowl of ice water. The ice water stops the cooking, so it stays bright green and a little crunchy.
Pour a little liquid into a hot pan after browning, and scrape up the brown bits stuck to the bottom. They melt into the liquid and give the dish its deep, savory flavor.
Cook vegetables gently over medium-low heat, often with a pinch of salt, until they're soft and see-through but not brown.
The brown bits stuck to a pan after food browns. Golden to dark brown is flavor; black is burnt. Deglazing lifts it into the sauce.
Plunge just-cooked food into ice water to stop the cooking, so vegetables stay crisp and bright.
The temperature where a fat starts to smoke and break down. Past it, oil tastes harsh and can catch fire.
Strong-smelling vegetables, like onion, garlic, celery, and ginger, cooked first to build a dish's flavor.
France's flavor base: onion, carrot, and celery, about two parts onion to one part each of the others.
Italy's flavor base: onion, carrot, and celery chopped fine and cooked slowly in olive oil.
The Spanish and Latin American flavor base: onion, garlic, and peppers, often with tomato, cooked gently in oil.
A seed that grows in a pod: beans, lentils, peas, and chickpeas. Dried, they keep for a year or more.
Spread dried beans or lentils out and look through them, taking out any tiny stones, dirt, or shriveled ones.
Boil dried beans for 2 minutes, turn off the heat, cover them, and leave them an hour. It's almost as good as soaking overnight.
A full, rolling boil, with big bubbles across the whole pot. Red kidney beans need 10 minutes of it to be safe.
Cooking a grain in just enough liquid for it to drink all of it, so nothing is drained.
A grain toasted in fat before the liquid goes in, then cooked with the lid on until every grain is separate.
A boneless piece of fish cut from along the backbone, with or without its skin.
Thin, soft bones in a row down the thick end of a fish fillet. Feel for them with your fingertips and pull them out with tweezers.
Cook food in the hot, wet air above boiling water, with a lid on. The gentlest way to cook fish and vegetables.
When cooked fish is pressed with a fork, it separates into layers called flakes. Flaking is one sign fish is done.
Food sealed in folded parchment and baked, so it steams in its own juices. French cooks call it en papillote.
Make shallow cuts across the surface of food, often in a crosshatch, without cutting all the way through. It lets fat run out, flavor soak in, or heat reach the middle.
Cook something fatty slowly so its fat melts out and collects in the pan, leaving the skin or meat crisp.

Mix something gently into a batter by scooping the spatula down to the bottom of the bowl and turning the batter over on top, then giving the bowl a quarter turn. It mixes without stirring out the air or crushing soft pieces.
